narrative:
The weather story Wednesday was unseasonable heat, and it is again today and Friday. Temperatures were near or above record levels Wednesday and will be through Friday. Isolated afternoon thunderstorms are possible both days. This weekend we make an impressive transition to a cool Labor Day. A front moves through Saturday, but the big cooldown waits until Sunday night. Widely scattered thunderstorms accompany the frontal passage Saturday, but more widespread showers lead the cool push late Sunday. Labor Day will feel like the end of summer, but it's not.

Near-record heat continues, and the atmosphere is dry aloft, so an isolated afternoon thunderstorm is the most we'll see. Friday brings a subtle change as the high slides offshore and a cold front approaches from the Ohio Valley. The heat holds. Isolated afternoon thunderstorms are again possible. Saturday the front crosses the mountains. Widely scattered showers and thunderstorms linger into the evening. It's not record levels but still an unseasonably warm, muggy September day. Sunday is the real changeover. A strong high building over the Great Lakes pushes cool air down the eastern side of the Appalachians, and periods of rain with some thunder develop, mostly in the afternoon. The temperature drop is impressive. Labor Day is cloudy and cool with a northeast breeze. Fog, drizzle, and light rain favor the east side of the Appalachians, mostly in the morning. Tuesday is warmer by afternoon with isolated afternoon thundershowers. Warmth returns Wednesday. Detailed forecast discussion and analysis is only available to RaysWeather supporters. All Photos Submit Photo Latest Insights August 2026 Recap First Weekend Flooding The story all spring and into the beginning of summer had been dry, dry, dry. Drought was just about the only weather story for the first third of summer, but July and August have bucked that trend with gusto. After July ended rather wet, the first weekend of August brought home isolated pockets of 5"+ for a handful of locations across the Ray's Weather coverage region. The most notable pocket of rain was in northeastern Surry County, where 8-10"+ fell on the 1st and 2nd, producing destructive flash flooding in Mount Airy. The city's public works fleet sustained several million dollars worth of damage from the fast-rising floodwaters, and a handful of nearby businesses experienced damage as well. Blowing Rock also saw brief flash flooding that weekend, with training thunderstorms (storms repeatedly moving over the same spot) dropping a localized 5-7 inches of rain while Boone recieved just under 3. No notable damage was reported from the Blowing Rock area, although there was one report of a small amount of water on a ground floor. Wet Summer... For Some Meteorological summer spans the months of June, July, and August, meaning we can now look back on the season as a whole. While temperatures were above normal (but not by a significant margin), precipitation varied by location. This should not come as a surprise, as the vast majority of summertime precipitation comes from afternoon & evening showers & thunderstorms, which are incredibly hit-or-miss. A few miles difference can mean a few inches of rain, which adds up over the course of a summer. Typically, far southwestern North Carolina tends to be the wettest place not only in the state, but in the entire Eastern US. This was not the case this summer, as the maps below show. The first map shows the departure from normal for June 1st to August 31st. Look down near Nantahala National Forest and Brevard, where multiple stations were over 6 inches below average on summer precipitation. Conversely, most stations along and north of Interstate 40 were 2 to 4 inches above average. Highlands, Brevard, Waynesville, and Cullowhee falling shy of Boone's summer total is not something we see often. Highlands recieving less than Asheville is even more surprising, given that Asheville lies in one of the driest areas of the state, the French Broad River Valley, while Highlands lies in a rainforest averaging nearly 90 inches of rain per year. The map below shows total precipitation for the summer. Year-to-date precipitation totals are still behind schedule at all locations in our region... except Marshall in Madison County, which is an inch ahead. Much of Avery County as well as Brevard and Highlands are over 10 inches below what the average year-to-date precipitation should be through the end of August. The Foothills lie 6 to 10 inches behind. Given the El Niño conditions, the late fall and winter period may bring an opportunity to recoup some of that. But, September does not tend to be an especially wet month unless a tropical system moves through, and the tropics have been very quiet thus far. We are approaching the modern record for the deepest run into a year without a storm reaching hurricane strength (the record - Sept. 11th, dating back over 60 years). Looks Like Summer Our monthly bar graph feature for August goes to North Wilkesboro, where temperatures were about where you'd expect them to be in the afternoons. North Wilkesboro did manage to go 31 for 31 on high temperatures at or above 80 degrees (not unusual - the average is 27 days above 80), but only 5 days surpassed 90 degrees, 3 below average. A far cry from last August, which had a remarkable 14 days with high temperatures below 80 degrees. Minimum temperatures were more notably above normal, with 15 lows of 70 or greater and only 1 low below 60 degrees. Temperatures Monthly mean temperatures were above average across the board. The only exceptions on above average lie with a handful of stations that managed below average mean high temperature for the month (Jefferson, Sparta, and Marshall), but low temperatures were above average without exception. Averaging everything out showed generally 1 to 4 degrees above average, again mostly thanks to warm low temperatures. Town by town specifics lie below.
